ENG0300 Reading Lab/Visual & Data

Week 7 · Skill Lab

Visual & Data Integration

Read charts, tables, and diagrams accurately, connect them to the text they accompany, and combine information from more than one source.

By the end of this lab you will be able to

  • ✓Read a chart's title, labels, and units before interpreting any value
  • ✓State what a figure shows without going beyond it
  • ✓Connect a figure to the claim in the text it accompanies
  • ✓Combine a text and a figure to answer a question neither answers alone

Course outcomes covered

  • Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, or timelines) and connect it to the related text
  • Integrate information from multiple texts or sources on the same topic

From the ENG0300 course syllabus.

1Learn

How this skill works

Read this first. Everything after it assumes these ideas.

Read the frame before you read the numbers

Most mistakes on chart questions happen before any thinking about the data, because the reader jumped to the tallest bar without checking what is being measured.

  • Title — what is this figure about?
  • Axis labels — what does each direction represent?
  • Units — dollars, percent, minutes, thousands? A percent chart and a count chart answer different questions.
  • Time span — what period is covered, and does the text discuss the same period?
  • Source note — where did the data come from, and does the text cite the same source?

Test tip

Say out loud what the figure shows in one sentence before you look at the question. If you cannot, you are not ready to answer, no matter how clear the bars look.

The figure and the text do different jobs

A figure and its surrounding text are not two copies of the same information. The text usually makes a claim; the figure usually supplies the measurement behind it. Questions turn on the relationship between them.

Question typeWhat it asksWhere to look
Read a valueWhat was the figure for a particular category?The figure alone
Compare valuesWhich is larger, and by how much?The figure alone
ConnectWhich detail in the chart supports the author's point?Text first, then figure
IntegrateWhat can be concluded from the chart and the text together?Both — the answer is in neither alone

What a figure cannot tell you

Charts invite conclusions they do not support. A chart shows what happened; it rarely shows why, and it never shows what will happen next unless the text says so.

  • A chart shows association, not cause. Two lines rising together do not establish that one caused the other.
  • A chart covering three years does not establish a long-term trend.
  • A chart of percentages hides the size of the group. Fifty percent of six people is three.
  • If the answer choice contains information not in the figure and not in the text, it is wrong regardless of how sensible it sounds.

Integrating more than one source

The final outcome of this course asks you to combine sources. When two sources address one topic, work through them in order: what does each say, where do they agree, where do they differ, and what can you conclude only by holding both at once?

  • Check whether the sources measure the same thing over the same period. Often they do not, and that is the answer.
  • Agreement between two independent sources strengthens a conclusion.
  • A disagreement is information. Ask what would explain it before deciding one source is wrong.
2See It

A worked example

Watch the reasoning before you try it. Notice the order of the moves — that order is the skill.

Connecting a chart to the argument beside it

The Cost of Getting There

Data / Charts125 words

When a training program reports its completion rate, the number is usually explained in terms of academics: the material was too hard, or students arrived underprepared. Program staff who track the reasons students actually give tell a different story.

In an exit survey at one workforce program, students who withdrew were asked to identify the primary reason. Academic difficulty appeared, but it was not the largest category. Transportation and schedule conflicts together accounted for more than half of all withdrawals.

The distinction matters because it points to different fixes. A program that believes its students are underprepared invests in tutoring. A program that knows its students cannot reliably get to class invests in bus passes, evening sections, and attendance policies that survive a missed shift.

Original passage and figure — BEOC Academic Bridge

The question

Which detail in the figure most directly supports the author's point in paragraph 2?

Thinking it through

  1. 1

    Read the frame first.

    Title: primary reason for withdrawing, one program's exit survey. Units: share of withdrawals, in percent. One program, one survey — so conclusions cannot extend past that.

  2. 2

    Restate the author's point in paragraph 2.

    Two claims: academic difficulty is not the largest category, and transportation plus schedule conflicts together exceed half.

  3. 3

    Check the first claim against the figure.

    Academic difficulty is 16 percent. Transportation is 31 and schedule conflict is 24, both larger. The claim holds.

  4. 4

    Check the second claim by combining bars.

    31 plus 24 is 55 percent. That is more than half, so "more than half" is exact rather than loose. This combination is the strongest support.

  5. 5

    Guard against the overreach.

    I cannot conclude that transportation causes withdrawals at other programs, or that bus passes would fix it. The figure reports reasons students gave, at one program.

The answer

Transportation at 31 percent and schedule conflict at 24 percent sum to 55 percent — more than half of all withdrawals — while academic difficulty accounts for 16 percent. That combination supports both halves of the author's claim.

Take this with you

When text says two categories together exceed some threshold, add the bars and check. That arithmetic is the support the question is asking about.

Your turn, with support

One question, with a hint available. Nothing here is graded.

Who Is Online at Home

Data / Charts65 words

Applications for jobs, benefits, and housing have moved online faster than home internet access has spread. A household without a home connection is not cut off entirely — phones fill part of the gap — but filling out a long form, uploading a document, or joining a video appointment on a phone is meaningfully harder than doing it on a computer with a fixed connection.

Original passage and figure — BEOC Academic Bridge

Question 1Chart / dataFoundation
Based on the figure, how much higher is the broadband subscription rate for households earning $100,000 and above than for households earning under $25,000?
4Practice

Practice on a full passage

A longer passage with several questions. Check each answer as you go.

When the Clinic Is Open

Health134 words

1A neighborhood clinic tracked how often its appointment slots went unused across a full year, sorted by the time of day the appointment had been scheduled.

2Staff had expected the worst performance in the earliest slots, on the assumption that patients would struggle to arrive before work. The data did not support that expectation. The 8 a.m. slots were among the better-attended hours. Midday performed worst by a wide margin.

3The explanation the clinic settled on was that patients who could come at 8 a.m. were arranging their day around the visit deliberately, while a midday appointment competed directly with a work shift that most patients could not leave without losing pay.

4The clinic responded by shifting several midday slots into an evening block. It has not yet published results for the evening hours.

Original passage and figure — BEOC Academic Bridge

Question 1Chart / dataFoundation
According to the figure, which time slot went unused most often?
Question 2Chart / dataTABE Ready
Which statement about the figure supports the author's point in paragraph 2 that staff expectations were wrong?
Question 3Multiple choiceChallenge
Which conclusion is NOT supported by the passage and the figure together?
5Challenge

A harder, TABE-style set

Denser text and less obvious answers — closer to what the test will ask of you.

Read both texts and the figure before you answer. Before you combine them, check what each source actually counts — most of these items turn on it.

Text A: Spring Report to the Pantry Board

Data / Charts155 words

1This spring was the busiest stretch our pantry has had since it opened. Visits held fairly steady from January through March, then jumped in April and stayed high through June. Between March and June, monthly visits grew by more than half.

2The figure below shows every visit recorded at our sign-in table this year, month by month. The pattern is hard to miss. Once April arrived, the monthly count never came close to its winter level again.

3The message for the board is simple: we are serving far more families than we were in the winter. By the last Saturday in May, our shelves were nearly bare, and volunteers had to give half orders to the people at the end of the line.

4I am asking the board to approve a larger monthly food order starting in July, so that no one who waits in that line goes home with less than a full order.

Original passage and figure — BEOC Academic Bridge

Text B: Notes From the Sign-In Table

Informational168 words

1I have worked the sign-in table every Saturday since last fall, so I see nearly every household that comes through the door. The spring rush was real. In May, the line reached the corner more than once.

2The monthly totals leave out a change the pantry made on April 1. Until then, each household could pick up groceries once a month. Starting in April, households could come twice. Many people I signed in on the first Saturday of a month were back two weeks later.

3Last week I went back through the sign-in sheets and counted each household only once per month, no matter how many times it came. In March, 340 different households signed in. In June, 365 did.

4So we are seeing some new faces, and we are seeing familiar faces more often. Both mean more food going out the door. But they are not the same thing, and the board should know which one it is looking at before it decides how much to order.

Original passage — BEOC Academic Bridge

Question 1Chart / dataTABE Ready
In paragraph 1 of Text A, the coordinator writes that between March and June, "monthly visits grew by more than half." Which calculation from the figure correctly checks this claim?
Question 2Select all that applyChallenge
Which conclusions are supported by the texts and the figure together — conclusions you could not reach from any one source alone? Select all that apply.
Question 3Paired textChallenge
Text A treats the rising bars as proof that the pantry is "serving far more families." What does Text B add that the figure cannot show?
Question 4Short responseChallenge
6Answer Review

Why each answer is right or wrong

The reasoning behind every choice, including the ones designed to catch you.

Work through the practice first, then open a question below to see the full reasoning. Reading why a wrong answer is wrong is what stops you from choosing it again on the test.

Practice set

Q1According to the figure, which time slot went unused most often?▾

Correct answer: C. 12:00 p.m.

Why: The noon bar is the tallest at 29 percent, just above 2 p.m. at 26 percent.

Every choice, explained

  • A.8:00 a.m. — The lowest bar at 12 percent — the best-attended slot, not the worst.
  • B.10:00 a.m. — 17 percent, the second-lowest.
  • C.12:00 p.m. — Correct. 29 percent, the tallest bar in the figure.
  • D.4:00 p.m. — 19 percent, in the middle of the range.
Q2Which statement about the figure supports the author's point in paragraph 2 that staff expectations were wrong?▾

Correct answer: B. The 8 a.m. slot had the lowest unused rate of any time shown, while the two midday slots were highest.

Why: Staff expected the earliest slots to be worst. The figure shows 8 a.m. best at 12 percent and midday worst at 29 and 26 percent — the reverse of the expectation.

Every choice, explained

  • A.The 4 p.m. slot had a higher unused rate than the 8 a.m. slot. — True from the figure, but it does not address the expectation about early slots being worst.
  • B.The 8 a.m. slot had the lowest unused rate of any time shown, while the two midday slots were highest. — Correct. It contrasts exactly the hours the expectation was about.
  • C.Every slot had some unused appointments. — True and uninformative. It says nothing about which hours performed worse.
  • D.The unused rate declined between noon and 4 p.m. — True, but the decline after noon is not what the staff expectation concerned.
Q3Which conclusion is NOT supported by the passage and the figure together?▾

Correct answer: B. Moving midday slots to the evening has reduced the clinic's unused-slot rate.

Why: Paragraph 4 says the clinic made the change but has not published results for the evening block. The outcome is unknown, so no conclusion about it is supported.

Every choice, explained

  • A.Midday appointments at this clinic went unused more often than early-morning appointments. — Directly supported by the figure — 29 and 26 percent versus 12 percent.
  • B.Moving midday slots to the evening has reduced the clinic's unused-slot rate. — Correct — this is the unsupported one. The passage explicitly says results are not yet available.
  • C.The clinic's staff expectation about early appointments was not borne out by its own data. — Supported by paragraph 2 read against the figure.
  • D.The clinic attributed midday no-shows to conflicts with work shifts. — Supported by paragraph 3, which gives the clinic's explanation.

Challenge

Q1In paragraph 1 of Text A, the coordinator writes that between March and June, "monthly visits grew by more than half." Which calculation from the figure correctly checks this claim?▾

Correct answer: D. 520 − 340 = 180, and 180 is more than half of 340, so the claim is supported.

Why: Find the two months the claim names — March at 340 and June at 520 — and subtract: 520 − 340 = 180. Growing "by more than half" compares the increase to the starting value, and half of 340 is 170. Since 180 is more than 170, the figure supports the claim. Notice what the claim and the figure both count, though: visits.

Every choice, explained

  • A.520 − 310 = 210, and 210 is more than half of 310, so the claim is supported. — The conclusion is right, but the numbers are not. 310 is the January bar; the claim starts in March, so the starting value must be 340.
  • B.480 − 340 = 140, and 140 is less than half of 340, so the claim is not supported. — 480 is the April bar. The claim runs to June, so the ending value must be 520. Stopping one month early makes a supported claim look unsupported.
  • C.520 − 340 = 180, but 180 is less than half of 520, so the claim is not supported. — The subtraction is right, but the comparison uses the wrong base. Growth is measured against where visits started, 340 in March, not where they ended. Half of 340 is 170, and 180 is more than that.
  • D.520 − 340 = 180, and 180 is more than half of 340, so the claim is supported. — Correct. March is 340 and June is 520, an increase of 180. Half of 340 is 170, so an increase of 180 is more than half.
Q2Which conclusions are supported by the texts and the figure together — conclusions you could not reach from any one source alone? Select all that apply.▾

Correct answer: A. Visits grew by 180 between March and June, while the number of different households grew by only 25. • C. The biggest one-month jump in visits came in April, the first month households were allowed a second visit.

Why: A combined conclusion needs a piece from each source. Choice A takes visits from the figure and households from Text B. Choice C takes the April jump from the figure and the April 1 rule change from Text B. Choice B is true but needs only the figure, and choices D and E go beyond anything either source says.

Every choice, explained

  • A.Visits grew by 180 between March and June, while the number of different households grew by only 25. — Correct. The 180 comes from the figure (520 − 340) and the 25 from Text B (365 − 340). Neither source has both numbers.
  • B.June had more recorded visits than any other month from January through June. — True, but the figure alone shows it: June's bar, at 520, is the tallest. It does not need either text, so it is not a combined conclusion.
  • C.The biggest one-month jump in visits came in April, the first month households were allowed a second visit. — Correct. The figure shows the biggest jump, from 340 to 480, arriving in April, and only Text B says April is when households could first come twice.
  • D.Visits rose this spring because more families in the neighborhood lost work. — Neither source mentions anyone losing work. This reads a cause into the pattern and supplies it from outside knowledge.
  • E.Visits will stay above 500 a month for the rest of the year. — Both sources stop at June. A figure cannot tell you what happens after the last month it shows, and neither text predicts it.
Q3Text A treats the rising bars as proof that the pantry is "serving far more families." What does Text B add that the figure cannot show?▾

Correct answer: B. It explains that the figure counts visits, not households: from April on, one household could come twice a month, and the number of different households rose only from 340 to 365.

Why: The figure measures visits. Text A reads visits as families; Text B shows why that reading fails after April 1, when one household could account for two visits. Visits rose by 180 while different households rose by 25, so most of the extra visits were return trips. Checking whether two sources measure the same thing is often the whole answer.

Every choice, explained

  • A.It confirms that the pantry was busier in the spring than in the winter. — Text B does agree — "The spring rush was real" — but the figure already shows a busier spring. This adds nothing the bars cannot show.
  • B.It explains that the figure counts visits, not households: from April on, one household could come twice a month, and the number of different households rose only from 340 to 365. — Correct. The figure has no way to show who made each visit. Text B supplies the rule change and the household counts that reveal the difference between visits and families.
  • C.It shows that the coordinator's visit counts are wrong and that the pantry was not really busier this spring. — Text B never disputes the counts. Its March total of 340 households matches the 340 visits in the figure, because each household could come only once that month.
  • D.It shows that visits will drop once families no longer need a second trip each month. — Neither source says the twice-a-month rule will end or predicts what visits will do next. This goes beyond both texts.
Q4In three or four sentences, write a conclusion about the pantry's spring that could not be reached from Text A, Text B, or the figure alone. Use at least one number from the figure and one from Text B.▾

Model response: The pantry did get much busier this spring, but mostly because the same households came more often, not because many more households came. The figure shows monthly visits rising from 340 in March to 520 in June, an increase of 180. Text B explains that households could come twice a month starting in April, and that the number of different households grew only from 340 to 365, an increase of 25. The coordinator is right that more food is going out the door, but the claim that the pantry is "serving far more families" does not hold up once both sources are read together.

Why: A complete answer does three jobs: it states one conclusion, supports it with a number from the figure and a number from Text B, and shows why the two together say something neither says alone. The trap is writing Text A's conclusion, because the figure by itself leads straight to it.

7Mastery Check

Check yourself

A short formative check. It is not recorded — use it to decide whether to move on or review.

One short passage with a figure, four items. If you miss one, the review below each answer will tell you which part of the lesson to revisit.

Waiting for a Child-Care Spot

Data / Charts100 words

A neighborhood child-care center keeps a separate waiting list for each age group. In September, the director counted the families on each list so she could give parents an honest answer when they asked how long they might wait. The infant list was the longest by far. Infant rooms need the most staff for each child, so the center has the fewest infant spots to offer. From there, the lists grew shorter as the children got older. The director reminds parents that the counts change every month, as children move up to the next room and spots open behind them.

Original passage and figure — BEOC Academic Bridge

Question 1Chart / dataFoundation
What does the figure measure?
Question 2Chart / dataDeveloping
According to the figure, how many more families were waiting for an infant spot than for a toddler spot?
Question 3Chart / dataTABE Ready
Which information in the figure best supports the statement that "the lists grew shorter as the children got older"?
Question 4Multiple choiceTABE Ready
Which conclusion is NOT supported by the passage and the figure together?
8Write It

Now write it yourself

The same skill, going the other direction. Nothing here is submitted from this page — you will copy your paragraph into Brightspace when it is ready.

Writing what a chart showsBased on “When the Clinic Is Open”

The clinic figure showed unused appointment slots by time of day: 12 percent at 8 a.m., 17 percent at 10 a.m., 29 percent at noon, 26 percent at 2 p.m., and 19 percent at 4 p.m. Staff expected the early slots to be worst. They were the best.

Write one paragraph of five to seven sentences that does two jobs a data question always asks for. First, say what the figure shows, using at least two exact numbers and naming the trend rather than listing every bar. Second, say why it matters — what someone running that clinic should do differently because of it.

Be careful with the last part. The figure shows when slots went unused. It does not show why. The passage offers an explanation about work shifts; if you use it, say that it is the clinic's explanation, not something the chart proves.

Before you submit, check each one

Ticking these is for your own tracking. Nothing here is scored or recorded.

Sentence frames

Starters, not a template. Fill one in, change the wording to sound like you, or write past it entirely.

  • The figure shows ______, measured by ______.
  • The rate rises from ______ percent at ______ to ______ percent at ______.
  • The chart shows when, not why; the clinic's explanation is that ______.

0 words · 0 sentences(a rough count from end punctuation — a guide, not a rule)

What you type stays in this browser. It is not sent anywhere, not scored by software, and not seen by anyone until you paste it into Brightspace yourself.

Score your own draft

This is the same 10-point rubric attached to the Brightspace dropbox. Scoring yourself first is the fastest way to find what to fix. Your score here is yours alone — it is not recorded and it is not your grade.

Focus — 3 points

One clear controlling idea, stated early and held to. Every sentence belongs to that idea — nothing wanders off the question that was asked.

Evidence & Development — 3 points

Specific support from the passage — details, examples, or quoted words — and an explanation of what that support shows. Not just a detail dropped in and left alone.

Organization — 2 points

A sensible order a reader can follow, with transitions that signal how one sentence relates to the next. A beginning, a middle, and an ending that lands.

Conventions — 2 points

Complete sentences, subject-verb agreement, capitalization, and end punctuation. Errors do not stop a reader from understanding you.

Score all four strands to see your total.

▸ Show a strong example▾ Hide the example

Watch the fifth sentence in particular. Refusing to overclaim is a skill the test rewards and most writers skip.

The figure shows how often a clinic's appointment slots went unused over one year, sorted by the time each appointment was scheduled. The rate is lowest first thing in the morning, at 12 percent for the 8 a.m. slots, and peaks at 29 percent around noon before falling back to 19 percent by 4 p.m. That pattern is the opposite of what the clinic's staff expected, since they had assumed the earliest appointments would be the hardest for patients to keep. A clinic looking at this should move slots out of the middle of the day, which is what this one did when it opened an evening block. The chart shows when slots went unused, though, not why; the explanation about midday appointments competing with unpaid time off work is the clinic's reasoning, not something the bars establish. The clinic has not yet published results for the evening slots, so whether the change worked is still an open question.

Which sentence earns which strand

  1. The figure shows how often a clinic's appointment slots went unused over one year, sorted by the time each appointment was scheduled.

    Focus — Says what is being measured before quoting a single number. A reader who does not know the units cannot judge the numbers.

  2. The rate is lowest first thing in the morning, at 12 percent for the 8 a.m. slots, and peaks at 29 percent around noon before falling back to 19 percent by 4 p.m.

    Evidence & Development — Three exact figures used to describe a shape — down, up, down — rather than reciting all five bars in a row.

  3. That pattern is the opposite of what the clinic's staff expected, since they had assumed the earliest appointments would be the hardest for patients to keep.

    Evidence & Development — Connects the figure to the text beside it. Integration is the skill being assessed, not chart-reading alone.

  4. A clinic looking at this should move slots out of the middle of the day, which is what this one did when it opened an evening block.

    Organization — The why it matters half, and it is actionable. A data paragraph that stops at description has answered half the question.

  5. The chart shows when slots went unused, though, not why; the explanation about midday appointments competing with unpaid time off work is the clinic's reasoning, not something the bars establish.

    Organization — The limit of the evidence, stated plainly. This sentence is what separates a careful reader from a confident one.

  6. The clinic has not yet published results for the evening slots, so whether the change worked is still an open question.

    Conventions — Accurate to the passage, complete, and correctly punctuated — and it ends on the honest note rather than a manufactured conclusion.
